summary: An FYI document with biographies of members of the IAB, the IESG, and the IRSG. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1336.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a "meet the team" page for the people who guided the Internet.

questions: who were the iab and iesg members in 1991
subtitle: Biographies of the Internet's leadership in 1991.

tldr.problem: The Internet had grown to thousands of networks with hundreds of thousands of users, but most people did not know who the volunteer leaders managing it were or how they came to this work.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1251 collects biographies of 18 key people who served on the IAB (Internet Activities Board), IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group), and IRSG (Internet Research Steering Group), telling their backgrounds, careers, and thoughts on the Internet's growth.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was replaced by RFC 1336, which updated the list of leaders as roles changed.

facts.label: NSFNET traffic growth
facts.value: 194 million to 5.9 billion packets in 2.4 years

today: RFC 1336 replaced RFC 1251 with an updated list of leadership biographies as the Internet continued to grow and roles changed.

sections.title: Internet Leadership and Contributors
sections.content:
By 1991, the Internet had grown from a small research experiment to a network of thousands of machines serving hundreds of thousands of users. This growth was not automatic: volunteers spending considerable time managing networks, coordinating standards, and organizing meetings made it possible. The Internet Activities Board (IAB), the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) of the IETF, and the Internet Research Steering Group (IRSG) of the IRTF were the bodies that guided the Internet's evolution.

RFC 1251 credits these leaders by publishing their biographies, so that the user community would know who was working behind the scenes. The RFC notes that early IETF meetings had only 20 or so people, but by 1991 the community had grown to several hundred members across many working groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says: "Thank you to the volunteers who run the Internet." It gives the backgrounds of 18 people in the IAB, IESG, and IRSG, so the Internet community could see who was leading them and where they came from.

sections.title: Internet Activities Board Members
sections.content:
The IAB is the overall leadership and strategy body for the Internet. RFC 1251 includes biographies of eight IAB members, including chairs and senior architects. Key figures include:

  • Vinton Cerf, IAB Chairman, who developed TCP/IP at Stanford with funding from DARPA and later managed the Internetting program at DARPA.
  • Robert Braden, IAB Executive Director, who coordinated DARPA networking research, edited the Host Requirements RFCs, and worked on TCP/IP at UCLA since the early 1970s.
  • David Clark, IRTF Chairman, who led TCP development at MIT and chaired the IAB from 1981 to 1990, focusing on high-speed networking and congestion control.
  • Several others who contributed to routing, security, X.500 directory services, and the growth of the NSFNET.

Their biographies show how the early Internet was built by academic researchers with DARPA and NSF support, many of whom stayed involved as the network grew from tens of nodes to thousands.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB members are the senior architects. Vint Cerf invented TCP/IP. Bob Braden coordinated research at UCLA. David Clark led work at MIT on making the network fast. They explain how they got into networking from the very beginning and what they think the Internet will do next.

sections.title: IETF Area Directors and IESG Members
sections.content:
The IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) manages the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), which develops protocols and standards. RFC 1251 includes biographies of IESG area directors covering:

  • Security (Stephen Crocker, who initiated the Network Working Group and the RFC series at UCLA in 1968)
  • Routing and Internet Services (Noel Chiappa, who conceived the multi-protocol backbone)
  • Applications (Russell Hobby, who worked on Point-to-Point Protocol at UC Davis)
  • Network Management (James Davin)
  • OSI Integration (Ross Callon)

Each biography shows their experience building networks, their current roles, and their vision for the Internet's future. Common themes include scaling to millions of hosts, security, and balancing TCP/IP with OSI standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF area directors are the engineers building the protocols. Stephen Crocker started the RFC series. Noel Chiappa invented routers that could handle multiple types of networks. Russell Hobby worked on protocols for connecting computers over phone lines. They share their thoughts on what the Internet still needs to solve.

sections.title: Perspectives on Internet Growth
sections.content:
Each biography includes the person's own reflection on how the Internet had grown and what lay ahead. Common observations across the 1991 biographies include:

  • Growth rate: The NSFNET backbone traffic went from 194 million packets in August 1988 to 5.9 billion packets in January 1991—a 30-fold increase in just over 2 years.
  • Internationalization: The Internet was expanding from a US-centric network to a global one, with connections forming in Europe, the Pacific, Australia, and South America.
  • Commercialization: The Internet was transitioning from purely academic and government use to commercial services (MCI Mail, vendors entering the market).
  • Scaling challenges: Multiple contributors expressed concern that the current Internet architecture (routing tables, addressing, protocol scalability) was approaching limits and would need rethinking.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1991, the Internet was growing faster and faster. Traffic was doubling every few months. Countries around the world were connecting. Companies were starting to use it. But the leaders worried: Would the old addressing system break? Would routing tables get too big? Could the architecture handle becoming truly global?

sections.title: Diversity of Backgrounds and Disciplines
sections.content:
The 18 people profiled came from diverse backgrounds: MIT, Stanford, UCLA, Yale, Bell Labs, DARPA, NSF, Digital Equipment Corporation, Bolt Beranek and Newman, SRI, and universities across North America. They had expertise in operating systems, routers, cryptography, network management, file transfer, email, and distributed systems.

What unified them was a shared belief that open collaboration was more powerful than competition. Robert Braden noted that the IAB worked informally and valued consensus. David Clark reflected that the Internet's fundamental success came from the community of researchers who believed in collaboration and shared the protocols openly—not through corporate competition or standardized committees.

By 1991, the community was being tested: funding agencies were shifting toward commercial competition, and the old academic model was under strain. Yet the biographies show a group still committed to making the Internet work for everyone.
sections.plainLanguage: These 18 people came from different universities and companies, but they shared a belief: collaboration works better than competition. They all believed in sharing ideas openly and working together, which was why the Internet succeeded.

references.text: Malkin, G., "Who's Who in the Internet: Biographies of IAB, IESG and IRSG Members", RFC 1251, FYI 9, August 1991.
